extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in media criticism; journalists and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the quality, accuracy, and independence of news reporting, with attention to the influence of press releases, wire copy, resource constraints, and claims about objectivity. Useful for critics, editors, and journalists evaluating news output or newsroom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth / factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism’s primary purpose is to tell the truth; 'truth' is used to mean factual accuracy (as distinct from interpretative veracity) and the journalist’s duty is 'to write what this journalist sees in reality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies argues that if journalism's goal is truth, journalists must 'check and to reject whatever is not true.' The review notes some blurring between cold fact and perspective but treats factual accuracy as central to the standard of good reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and source-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must gather sources and verify facts; failure to check undermines truth-telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies illustrates lack of verification with a trainee's week: 48 stories in five days, 26 people interviewed (only 4 face-to-face), and 93.5% office time — showing there is often insufficient time to properly gather sources and verify facts. The reviewer emphasizes that those who influence public opinion 'are not checking their sources.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'churnalism' (over-reliance on recycled material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism should not consist largely of copying wire agency copy or press releases ('churnalism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study cited found 60% of stories in four UK nationals 'consisted wholly or mainly of wire copy and/or PR material' and only 12% were generated entirely by reporters. The page warns that reporters often copy press releases, replacing the company line with their own byline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward press releases / PR material
rubrics_metrics.description: Press-release and PR-related material are inherently biased and should be viewed skeptically by journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies documents that PR influence has risen as newsrooms have contracted; many reporters accept PR material uncritically. Good practice: treat PR material as a starting point to be checked and independently verified, not as finished copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient time and resources for reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality reporting requires adequate staffing, time in the field, and resources; severe cutbacks and higher output expectations undermine reporting quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review links newsroom cuts, fewer journalists, and demands for more stories to declines in verification and original reporting. Examples: radical downsizing of wire services, lack of foreign correspondents (130 countries without TV wire representation), and the trainee example above demonstrate how resource constraints impair journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from corporate/ownership pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should resist corporate takeover pressures that prioritize profit over vigilance and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies argues 'Flat Earth news has gone global' because of takeover by corporate owners, cuts in staff, increased output, and the collapse of old supply lines — all of which shift priorities from truth-telling to profit-making ('save money, make money, make friends, hurt enemies').

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of pure objectivity and the necessity to acknowledge selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of pure objectivity is impractical; reporting necessarily involves selection and interpretation, so claiming neutrality can mask failure to tell the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies criticizes the 'safety net' of 'giving both sides of the story' as sometimes an excuse not to tell the truth. The reviewer notes ambiguity in Davies' stance but agrees selection is inherent in reporting and that there are often more than two sides to a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / reporter-generated material
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable proportion of stories should be generated by reporters themselves rather than sourced from wires or PR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cited study of four UK nationals found only 12% of stories where all material was generated by reporters, implying that higher shares of original reporting are a marker of better journalistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate international/newsgathering presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust foreign reporting and wire representation are necessary for comprehensive and accurate international news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies points out that 130 countries have no TV wire representation, contributing to gaps in coverage (e.g., limited reporting from Darfur, Congo, Sudan). The guidance is that underfunded international bureaus lead to reliance on inadequate substitutes for on-the-ground reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about limitations and interpretative choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should be transparent about the limits of their reporting and acknowledge when pieces involve interpretation rather than pure fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review highlights that readers often consume 'ready-made opinions and interpretations' instead of raw facts; transparency about selection and perspective helps readers understand how conclusions were reached and mitigates misleading claims of neutrality.
